analysis.one_liner: Restricts employers' use of AI to hire, fire, discipline, and manage workers, with a right to a human manager.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 13 cosponsors in December 2025, sits in three House committees with no action taken since its referral, and no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Employers with 11 or more workers could no longer let a software system alone decide who gets hired, fired, disciplined, paid, or scheduled. Any AI system used in those decisions would need pre-deployment testing for bias, annual independent audits made public, plain-language notice to workers, a human double-check of the machine's output, and a way for the worker to dispute and appeal the decision to a person. Workers being managed by software could opt out and be assigned a human manager instead. The bill also creates a new Technology and Worker Protection Division inside the Labor Department, lets workers and unions sue for money damages, and voids forced-arbitration clauses for these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at medium and large employers who are hired, scored, disciplined, or scheduled by algorithms — including app-based and temp workers — get notice, an explanation, a human check, and a way to appeal. People rejected by biased hiring software could sue for damages, and unions could sue on their behalf.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers screened or managed by algorithms

how_it_helps.text: An employer may not rely exclusively on an automated decision system for any hiring, firing, discipline, pay, scheduling, or promotion decision, and may use one only if it has been tested for efficacy and for discrimination under federal civil rights, age, disability, genetic, and pregnancy-discrimination laws [S2].

Every system used on workers must be independently tested at least once a year for discriminatory impact, with the results made public, and the employer must give workers plain-language documentation of how the system scored them within 7 days of a decision, plus a right to dispute and appeal to a human [S2].
A worker managed through an automated system can opt out and be managed by a human manager instead, and retaliation against workers who complain is prohibited [S2].

Workers and labor unions can sue violators for actual or treble damages plus statutory damages of $5,000–$40,000 per violation, get attorney's fees, and cannot be blocked by pre-dispute arbitration agreements or class-action waivers; state attorneys general and privacy regulators may also sue on residents' behalf [S2].

The bill creates a Technology and Worker Protection Division in the Department of Labor, with advisory boards that must include labor-organization and worker representatives, to write rules and investigate employers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more workers and the vendors selling them AI hiring and management tools, which would bear testing, annual third-party audits, disclosure, documentation, training, and litigation costs — including statutory damages of at least $5,000 per violation, indexed to inflation. Government employers, including federal and state agencies, are covered too.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using AI in worker decisions

drawbacks.text: Compliance is expensive and operationally hard: employers must commission pre-deployment validation, yearly independent bias audits made public, detailed disclosures before job applications, 7-day plain-language documentation of every algorithmic decision, training for system operators, and separate human corroboration and appeal tracks for each affected worker [S2].

Per-worker statutory damages ($5,000–$20,000 per violation, up to $40,000 when willful or repeated, plus treble actual damages and mandatory attorney's fees) give plaintiffs' lawyers a strong financial incentive to sue, and the bill voids arbitration and class-action waivers for these claims, which employers' groups typically call a litigation magnet [S2].

The smallest employers are exempt (the bill covers employers with 11 or more workers), but firms just above that line face the same audit and documentation machinery as large corporations, with no scaled-down path [S2].

The ban on exclusive automation and the opt-out to a human manager could be difficult for app-based scheduling and staffing businesses whose model is built on algorithmic dispatch, and the bill does not explain how to staff human reviewers at scale [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address a real and growing practice: scoring job applicants and managing workers by software that workers cannot see or question. The disclosure, human-review, and audit requirements are the honest cost of that transparency, and the small-employer exemption keeps the burden off the tiniest firms. The main legitimate worry is the damages regime: per-violation statutory damages plus fee-shifting and a class-action carve-out could produce litigation that outpaces the harms it remedies, and the human-oversight requirements are unfunded mandates the bill leaves each employer to figure out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 3, 2025 and sent to three House committees — Education and Workforce, House Administration, and Oversight — none of which has acted on it since, and no vote is scheduled [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici introduced the No Robot Bosses Act on December 3, 2025, joined by Reps. Deluzio and Moylan as original cosponsors [S2].

The bill was referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce and, in addition, to the Committees on House Administration and Oversight and Government Reform; no committee has reported or scheduled action on it since [S4].
The bill has 13 cosponsors, 12 Democrats and 1 Republican [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. The bill is pending, and employers using algorithmic management simply face no new federal rules while it sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill is pending

sides.party_line_note: Support so far is almost entirely Democratic (12 of 13 cosponsors), with one Republican; no one has spoken or voted against the bill because it has not reached a committee vote or the floor [S3].

industries.industry: AI hiring and workforce-management software vendors
industries.note: The bill's core customers' practices — scoring applicants, algorithmic scheduling, automated discipline — would require pre-deployment validation, annual public bias audits, disclosures, human corroboration, and appeal machinery, with statutory damages per affected worker. Vendors can comply only by rebuilding products around human oversight.

industries.industry: Large employers using algorithmic management (retail, warehousing, app-based and staffing platforms)
industries.note: They gain auditability and a documented defense against bias claims, but bear audit, disclosure, documentation, and litigation costs, and workers get an opt-out from algorithmic management entirely.

industries.industry: Independent algorithmic audit and compliance firms
industries.note: The bill creates a mandatory annual third-party testing market; any system used on workers must be independently audited for discriminatory impact at least yearly, with results published.

analysis.trajectory: Introduced in December 2025 with 14 total supporters and split across three committees, the bill is unlikely to get a standalone vote this session. Its realistic path is dying quietly in committee unless its provisions are folded into a larger workforce or AI package, which would require significant additional Republican support.
